newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Investors cautiously optimistic on Bhutto removal.
newsitem.headline: Investors cautiously optimistic on Bhutto removal.

text.p: The dismissal of Pakistan Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto won approval from Asian fund managers on Tuesday, but most plan to wait for further developments before reallocating regional investment portfolios.
"At first glance it's definitely positive, but we will have wait to see what happens in the February elections," said Anand Trivedi, fund manager with Credit Lyonnais in Hong Kong.
Pakistani president Farooq Leghari sacked Bhutto on Tuesday, accusing her three-year-old government of corruption and nepotism. Elections were called for February 3 next year.

Fund managers said they applauded Bhutto's removal and the end of an administration they said was characterised by ethnic violence, corruption, currency devaluations, inflation and high interest rates.

Pakistan's economy "was deteriorating very quickly and had reached a point where some radical action such as this was probably necessary," said Haresh Balani, Pakistan and India fund manager with Thornton Management (Asia) in Hong Kong.

But investment managers were uniformly cautious on the longer-term outlook, even though they said they expect a short-term rally on the Karachi bourse. The market was closed for a national holiday on Tuesday.
"That this happened has to be seen as good news, although one must temper one's view of Pakistan given its track record," Balani said.
Pakistan's official news agency APP said the president had appointed former parliament speaker Meraj Khalid as interim prime minister.
Khalid's performance, along with the overall composition of the new government, will be critical for investor sentiment, fund managers said.
"This government was, in the opinion of the market, very corrupt and because of this the economy was in a shambles," said Kalim Aziz, head of research at ING Barings in Karachi.
"The change in government and particularly the interim prime minister -- he is viewed as a relatively cleaner person -- will be very important," he said.
Aziz forecast an immediate short-term rally driven by local buying, which could attract foreign interest, and said the Karachi bourse presents a longer-term buying opportunity.

"People should start looking at their portfolios now," he said. "The market is very cheap on a fundamental basis, it's cheaper than it has been for four years. There is good earnings growth and good value in this market."

But fund managers said that in addition to the uncertainty surrounding the upcoming elections, they were anxious to see the outcome of talks to revive a stalled US$600 million standby loan as well as a review of the country's debt ratings by Moody's Investors Service Inc.
"You still have the basic economic problems irrespective of whether Bhutto goes," said Trivedi.
"Interest rates are going up. The economy is still fairly precarious. Things are not going to change overnight."
An apparent halt in a programme of privatisations, which appeared after the public sale of some of the Kottadu Power Company earlier this year, was also a disincentive to foreign investment.
"The local gas companies were meant to be privatised and also one of the electricity distribution companies, but nothing has happened," said one fund manager, who declined to be named.
"That's because the government failed to reshape the regulatory framework as a precursor to attracting foreign investors to consider taking a stake," he said.
